core.big_idea: Translation and textual study involve evidence-based judgments that should be explained without panic or overclaiming.

passages.reading_note: Observe public reading, explanation, and the goal of understanding.
Use the translation’s own footnote as a case study; do not settle the passage’s textual history from memory.
Use the translation’s own footnote as a second case study in transparent editorial notice.

core.metanarrative_position: Scripture received and understood: communities read inherited texts, translate or explain them, and evaluate manuscript evidence responsibly.
core.biblical_genre: Post-exilic narrative with textual-transmission and translation method

claims.statement: Nehemiah 8 depicts the law being read publicly and explained so that the people could understand.
Translation is the act of representing a source-language text in another language; interpretation is unavoidable but should be disciplined and transparent.
claims.interpretive_hinge: How lexical, grammatical, literary, and audience factors are weighed in a translation choice.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not describe any English translation as interpretation-free.

claims.statement: Textual criticism compares manuscript evidence to make reasoned judgments about earlier recoverable wording.
evidence_refs: Selected manuscript evidence; source review required
claims.interpretive_hinge: The age, quality, geographical distribution, and relationships of manuscripts and readings.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not claim that scholars simply vote, guess, or alter the Bible according to preference.

claims.statement: Visible translation footnotes about textual variants are evidence of transparency rather than proof that Scripture cannot be studied responsibly.
claims.credible_alternative: Critics may see prominent variants as evidence of uncertainty severe enough to weaken confidence, while some defenders minimise them too aggressively.
claims.interpretive_hinge: Whether transparent uncertainty in particular readings undermines or supports confidence in responsible textual study.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not say there are no meaningful variants, and do not say the entire text is therefore unknowable.

claims.statement: Students should calibrate confidence claim by claim and avoid both panic and inflated apologetic slogans.
claims.credible_alternative: Some teaching strategies avoid textual questions until advanced study; others use maximal-certainty claims to protect confidence.
claims.interpretive_hinge: Whether resilience is better formed by managed transparency or by withholding complexity.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not tell students that every textual question has a simple answer or that one footnote destroys Christian faith.

core.interpretation_skill: Distinguish translation choice, manuscript variant, textual judgment, and theological conclusion; calibrate confidence.

learning.foundation_objective: Explain the difference between translation and manuscript comparison and identify why both require disciplined judgment.
learning.extension_objective: Evaluate a real translation footnote, identify the evidence needed, and state a confidence level without panic or overclaiming.
know: Nehemiah 8 links reading and explanation with understanding.
Translations represent source-language texts in another language.
Manuscripts sometimes preserve different readings that require evaluation.
understand: Human judgment in transmission study does not mean arbitrary invention.
Transparent footnotes can strengthen responsible trust by showing where evidence is discussed.
practise: Read translation notes rather than ignore them.
Say “I do not know” when the evidence has not been studied.
become: A student who responds to textual questions with curiosity, method, and proportionate confidence.
success_evidence: The student defines translation and textual criticism separately.
The student audits one footnote without claiming more than it says.
The student identifies both a panic claim and an overconfident claim.

zero_prep_card.objective: Students distinguish translation from textual criticism and practise calibrated confidence using Bible footnotes.
zero_prep_card.read: Nehemiah 8:1-8; selected footnotes at Mark 16 and John 7-8
zero_prep_card.opening: Display two English translations of one ordinary sentence. Ask what can change while the same event is represented.
say: Nehemiah 8 joins reading, explanation, and understanding.
Translation asks how to represent words and meaning in another language.
Textual criticism asks which reading is best supported when manuscripts differ.
Honest footnotes are not a reason for panic, and confident claims still need evidence.
ask: What actions lead to understanding in Nehemiah 8?
How is translation different from manuscript comparison?
What does the footnote actually claim?
Which response is more responsible than denial or panic?
zero_prep_card.do: Complete the Translation and Manuscript Decision Lab using one selected footnote from the Bibles available.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray for courage to ask questions, patience with evidence, and honesty about uncertainty.

preparation.passage_context: Nehemiah 8 concerns post-exilic public Torah reading and explanation, not modern textual criticism. It supplies a theological starting point: understanding requires faithful reading and explanation. Modern manuscript examples require external historical study.
text_observations: The people gather and ask for the book of the law.
The text is read publicly and attention is emphasised.
Verse 8 joins clear reading or interpretation with giving the sense so people understand.
interpretation_notes: Do not use Nehemiah 8 as direct proof of one modern translation philosophy.
Use the actual footnotes in the edition present; do not reproduce long copyrighted translation text.
Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 are teaching cases, not permission to make unsourced claims about every manuscript.
theological_guardrails: Do not claim the original manuscripts are currently available for inspection.
Do not say variants never affect meaning; discuss scope case by case.
Do not build or destroy a doctrine solely on an unreviewed disputed reading.

likely_questions.question: Has the Bible been changed?
likely_questions.purpose: Distinguish copying variation from deliberate wholesale rewriting; say specific claims require examination of manuscript evidence.

likely_questions.question: Which English translation is perfect?
likely_questions.purpose: No translation is interpretation-free; compare purpose, method, and notes rather than declaring one infallible English edition.

family.title: Read the Footnote
family.parent_intro: This study treats translation notes as opportunities for careful learning rather than fear.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Read Nehemiah 8:5-8, then inspect one textual footnote in a family Bible.
Ask what the footnote states, what it does not state, and what further evidence would be needed.
Compare one short verse in two translations and list wording that changes and meaning that remains.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What is the difference between translation and manuscript comparison?
Why can transparency build rather than destroy trust?

interactive.title: Footnote Audit
interactive.instructions: Record the footnote’s exact claim, available evidence, missing evidence, and a calibrated conclusion.

family.weekly_action: Read one Bible footnote this week and write one honest question for later study.
family.prayer: God, give us understanding, patience with evidence, and humility when we do not yet know.
family.parent_note: Do not make a teenager defend the Bible under pressure; the goal is method and resilience, not winning a debate.

accessibility.reading_level: Teen discussion with technical terms defined and claims tested against context.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use precise language; define specialist terms and separate evidence from conclusion.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow written rather than spoken responses.
sensory_notes: No required role-play, public disclosure, or competitive performance.
non_reader_support: Provide concise claim cards or summaries without replacing the biblical text.

do_not_ask: Do not require a student to reveal private doubts or publicly defend family beliefs.
Do not shame students for using a different translation.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Normalise questions, separate evidence from loyalty, and provide a path for later research rather than forcing instant resolution.
